title: The family
description: Talk about the people you are related to, and say whose things are whose.
grammar: possessives, and the words for family
grammarNote: A possessive goes before the noun: mi casa, nuestro padre.

explanation.summary: Possessives say who something belongs to. They come before the noun and never take an article: mi casa, tu coche, nuestro perro. The family words are irregular in one way worth knowing: the same word means both a parent and a child.

sections.heading: The possessives
sections.body: Mi is my, tu is your, su is his or her or their, nuestro is our, vuestro is your (plural). They are the same for masculine and feminine nouns, and they go straight before the noun with no article: mi hermana, sus hijos.

sections.heading: Padre and padre
sections.body: Spanish has a word for a parent that is also a word for a child, and another that is only the parent. Padre means father and also father as a relative. Madre means mother. Hijo and hija mean son and daughter, and they are only ever children, never parents.

sections.heading: Who is su?
sections.body: Su means his, her, its, their, and you cannot tell which from the word alone. Spanish leans on the sentence: es su coche could be his car or her car. If you need to be clear, you say de él or de ella.

items.note: Masculine: el padre. It also means a priest, and a relative.
Masculine: el hijo. It is only ever a child.
Feminine: la hija. It is only ever a child.
Masculine: el hermano. The feminine is la hermana.
Masculine: el abuelo. The feminine is la abuela.
It goes before the noun: mi casa. It never takes an article.
It goes before the noun: nuestra casa. The feminine is nuestra.

drills.note: The possessive goes before the noun.
Su means his, her or their.
Hijo is only ever a child, and it takes an -s in the plural.
Nuestro changes to nuestros in front of a plural noun.
